# Letter of Aristeas Chapter 1 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal)
**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Greek MS | **Section:** The Origin of the Septuagint — Ptolemy Commissions the LXX

---

**1** Since I have gathered a memorable account of our visit to Eleazar the High Priest of the Jews, and since you, Philocrates, have shown such earnest zeal to hear about the law and divine affairs, I have undertaken to set this out clearly for you.

**2** I know you have a philosophical temperament, and that you consider it the highest honor to keep the mind free from material distractions and to reflect nobly on what is good and true.

**3** It is by the pursuit of this kind of life that I have become thoroughly devoted to such things — moved by reverence for the beauty of virtue and the glory of those who live by it.

**4** Your detailed prior knowledge and your dedication to philosophical study will both help you understand this account.

**5** At the time when our father Philocrates was rewarded for his devoted service to the king and we too were honored, I had the privilege of being present when Aristeas set out on his mission.

**6** Demetrius of Phalerum was at that time in charge of the royal library and had received large sums of money with the aim of collecting, if possible, all the books in the world.

**7** Through purchases and translations he assembled the collected works as best he could. When asked, 'How many thousands of books do you have?' he replied: 'About two hundred thousand, O king; I shall work diligently to bring the number to five hundred thousand in short order.'

**8** He also told me that books of the Jewish law were among those still needed, and others as well, and that they were worthy of being transcribed and placed in the royal library.

**9** 'What is there to prevent you from writing to the High Priest in Jerusalem and asking him to send men of the highest character, capable of interpreting the law?' I asked. 'I could then faithfully translate the copies for the royal library.'

**10** Demetrius was pleased to hear this and told the king. The king, having been informed, ordered letters to be sent to the High Priest, requesting that seventy-two elders — six from each tribe — be sent to him.

**11** I thought, Philocrates, that you would be very glad to hear of this. Before I begin the account, I should make clear the purpose of this great undertaking — it was for the sake of the Jewish law.

**12** Since God is the sovereign of all people, and since the same God who created us all maintains the world and provides for our needs, I resolved to make a plea on behalf of the Jewish captives.

**13** I held that those unjustly taken from their land deserved to go home, and that great glory would come to the king if he ordered their release.

**14** I went to the king and spoke on their behalf, saying: 'O king, the men brought here by force from Judea have served you and your father faithfully.'

**15** 'They are men of the highest virtue and devotion. I ask therefore that you grant them their freedom and write to those in charge throughout the kingdom to permit their return to their homeland.'

**16** The king was greatly pleased by my words and replied: 'It is fitting that those who have served faithfully should receive their freedom. I will write to all the governors throughout the kingdom, and to the tax collectors and administrators.'

**17** The king commanded that a proclamation be issued releasing all the Jewish captives — men, women, and children — and that each should receive their freedom.

**18** He also commanded that payment be made from the royal treasury for each person freed, and that their masters should receive fair compensation.

**19** The number of those set free was more than one hundred thousand.

**20** In addition to these, those serving in the army who had been brought there before the time of your father and were still in service were also to be set free.

**21** I have written out the full text of the decree so that its full scope may be understood.

**22** The Decree: 'Those who came into this land with our father Ptolemy on various occasions, or who were brought in under compulsion for military service, or who came in during the troubles that followed — all such persons shall receive their freedom.'

**23** 'It is my will that payment be made for each such person from the royal treasury, and that the masters who received them be compensated at the rate of twenty drachmas per person.'

**24** 'I am convinced that the liberation of so many people will please the God of the universe, who has maintained our reign in peace and in the highest renown throughout the world.'

**25** The officials reported to the king the total amount to be paid: one thousand four hundred and sixty talents.

**26** The king gave his approval at once: 'Let it be done, for the sake of our dignity and for the honor of God.'

**27** The captives were freed, and great rejoicing spread throughout the land, and many blessings were pronounced on the king.

**28** After this was accomplished, Demetrius raised the matter with the king again: 'It remains to send for the men who will translate the law from Jerusalem.'

**29** The king was pleased and said: 'Write a letter to the High Priest Eleazar and ask him to send six elders from each tribe — men of excellent character and wide learning — so that we may understand the law and translate it accurately.'

**30** I will transcribe here the full text of the letter that was sent.

**31** 'King Ptolemy to Eleazar the High Priest, greeting and good health. Since it has always been our policy to show kindness to all, and especially to men of noble character, and most of all to those of your nation, we have decided to take this opportunity to demonstrate our goodwill to all your people.'

**32** 'We have released from our realm more than one hundred thousand Jewish captives, paying their masters the appropriate price and making good any wrongs done.'

**33** 'Our purpose in this is to honor both you and God, whose law your people observe.'

**34** 'We have decided to have your law translated into Greek, knowing it will be of great benefit to all people.'

**35** 'We therefore ask you to send us six men from each of the twelve tribes — men of wisdom and learning, capable of translating the law with accuracy.'

**36** 'We believe that when this is accomplished it will greatly add to our credit, and we shall have done something noble.'

**37** 'We have sent gifts for the temple from our own resources, as is fitting.'

**38** Eleazar read the letter and was greatly pleased. He said to the messengers: 'I will respond to the king with all diligence.'

**39** He then chose seventy-two men, six from each tribe — men of excellent character, great learning, and deep piety.

**40** They were also greatly experienced in the law and well versed in the Greek language, for it was essential that they be able to render the Hebrew scriptures accurately into Greek.

**41** Their names were recorded, and I will supply the full list here so that you may know who these men were.

**42** From the tribe of Reuben: Joseph, Ezekiah, Zachariah, John, Hezekiah, Elisha. From the tribe of Simeon: Judas, Simon, Samuel, Adaeus, Mattathias, Eschlemias.

**43** From the tribe of Levi: Theodosius, Jason, Jesus, Theodotus, Jonathan, Dositheus. From the tribe of Judah: Caleb, Joseph, Simeon, Zachariah, Samuel, Selomias.

**44** And so with all the remaining tribes — six from each — until all seventy-two were appointed.

**45** They were sent to Alexandria with Eleazar's letter, bringing with them the sacred scrolls of the law — written in golden letters on beautifully prepared skins.

**46** When the king saw them, he was greatly pleased and asked them many questions about the law and the wisdom of their nation.

**47** He honored them greatly and prepared a magnificent feast in their honor, at which the wisest men of Egypt were also present.

**48** He asked the translators to answer the questions he would put to them, at the rate of one question per day during the feast.

**49** The king intended to test their wisdom and understanding of the law in this way.

**50** All who were present were amazed at the quality of their answers, and the king himself declared that he had never heard men answer so wisely.

**51** Before the translators arrived, however, the king had prepared magnificent gifts to send to the temple in Jerusalem.

**52** Among the gifts was a great table of gold and silver, overlaid with precious stones and of extraordinary workmanship.

**53** The craftsmen were the most skilled in all Egypt, and the king himself oversaw the work, insisting on the highest standards.

**54** The table was made to a size suitable for the temple sanctuary and was adorned with figures of every kind of fruit and flower.

**55** The table's border was decorated with a vine pattern — the tendrils of pure gold, and clusters of grapes formed from inlaid gems.

**56** At the corners were golden cups filled with incense, surrounded by wreaths of lilies and other flowers.

**57** The workmanship surpassed anything seen before, and when it was finished the king inspected it and expressed his satisfaction.

**58** He also had two golden bowls of great size prepared, with carved scenes depicting the history of the world from creation.

**59** These were to be used in the temple for the offering of incense, filled with the finest incenses of every kind.

**60** The king also sent golden vials, cups, and a vast quantity of fine linen and purple cloth for the temple service.

**61** He also sent pure golden incense burners and candelabra of the finest workmanship.

**62** There were thirty golden mixing bowls, twenty silver bowls, and goblets of fine crystal.

**63** The total value of the gifts was estimated at more than two hundred talents of gold.

**64** When the gifts were loaded onto the ships, the king himself came to the harbor to see them off.

**65** He also sent a personal letter to Eleazar, expressing his desire for the translation to proceed.

**66** In the letter the king asked Eleazar to pray for him and for his kingdom.

**67** Eleazar received the gifts with great joy and gave thanks to God for inspiring the king.

**68** He sent back with the messengers his warmest greetings and a letter of his own.

**69** He wrote: 'King Ptolemy, beloved of God, to Eleazar the High Priest, greetings.'

**70** The High Priest praised the king's generosity and spoke of the benefits of the translation.

**71** He said that the work of translating the divine law was of the greatest importance.

**72** He promised that the seventy-two translators would work with all diligence and faithfulness.

**73** He assured the king that the men chosen were of the highest character and wisdom.

**74** He described the beauty and orderliness of the temple and the holy city.

**75** He told of the daily sacrifices offered for the king and his household.

**76** He gave the names of the seventy-two translators and their tribal affiliations.

**77** He concluded with a blessing: 'May God guard you and preserve your kingdom in peace.'

**78** The letter was received with joy at the royal court, and great preparations were made.

**79** The king ordered a magnificent reception to be prepared for the translators.

**80** The harbor was decorated, and food and gifts were prepared for their arrival.

**81** For seven days before their arrival the city was in festive preparation.

**82** And on the day they arrived, a great crowd came to the harbor to meet them.

**83** The city of Jerusalem is situated in the midst of a great hill, and the temple is at the highest point.

**84** The city is not large in extent, but it is built on the summit of a hill of considerable size.

**85** The temple faces east, and the morning sun illuminates it when it rises.

**86** There is a great outer court, and within it are the courts for the priests and the Levites.

**87** The sanctuary itself is divided into the holy place and the most holy place.

**88** No one enters the most holy place except the High Priest, and only on the Day of Atonement.

**89** The altar of burnt offering stands in the middle of the outer court, a great structure of stone.

**90** The priests perform their service in complete silence, and with the greatest reverence.

**91** There is a constant supply of wood for the altar fires, and the fires burn night and day.

**92** The water supply of the temple is remarkable — springs of pure water well up within the temple precincts.

**93** The whole building is constructed of massive stone blocks, fitted together without mortar.

**94** The skill of the builders was extraordinary, and the temple is a marvel of human craftsmanship.

**95** There are chambers around the outer court where the temple vessels are stored.

**96** The vessels of gold and silver are of extraordinary beauty and craftsmanship.

**97** Everything in the temple is arranged with the greatest order and beauty.

**98** The priests who serve in the temple are men of great dignity and holiness.

**99** They are dressed in white linen garments of the finest quality.

**100** Their service is conducted with perfect silence and order.

**101** The sight of the temple service is so majestic that it fills the beholder with awe.

**102** Eleazar the High Priest presides over all the temple service with great dignity.

**103** His vestments are of extraordinary beauty and covered with precious stones.

**104** On his head he wears the golden diadem with the sacred Name engraved upon it.

**105** His breastplate contains twelve stones, one for each tribe of Israel.

**106** When the High Priest appears in his full vestments, he is a magnificent sight.

**107** The beauty of his appearance is beyond description, and all who see him stand in awe.

**108** The land surrounding Jerusalem is fertile and well-watered.

**109** The hills are covered with vines and olive trees and fig trees.

**110** The plains are rich in grain and produce of every kind.

**111** The people of the land are industrious and devoted to their God.

**112** Their laws govern every aspect of their lives, from the greatest matters to the smallest.

**113** They eat no food that has not been prepared according to their law.

**114** They observe the Sabbath with great strictness and do no work on that day.

**115** They observe the festivals of their law with joy and celebration.

**116** Their devotion to their law is the source of their strength as a people.

**117** They believe that the law was given to them by God himself through Moses.

**118** They regard the law as the greatest gift God has given to any people.

**119** Their wisdom comes from their constant study and practice of the law.

**120** All this I observed during my time in Jerusalem, and I was filled with admiration.

**121** Eleazar the High Priest is a man of great stature and beauty, and his bearing is dignified and noble.

**122** He welcomed us with great warmth and spoke to us about the law and the wisdom of God.

**123** He said: 'The law of God is the foundation of all wisdom, and those who live by it will know true happiness.'

**124** He spoke of the creation of the world and the wisdom with which God ordered it.

**125** He said: 'God made all things out of nothing, and he made them good, and he gave them to us to enjoy.'

**126** He spoke of the nature of God: 'God is one, and there is no other god besides him.'

**127** 'He is the creator of all things and the sustainer of all things, and he knows all things.'

**128** 'His wisdom is beyond all understanding, and his power is beyond all limitation.'

**129** He spoke of the law: 'Every commandment of the law has a reason and a purpose.'

**130** 'The laws about food teach us to control our desires and not to be enslaved by appetite.'

**131** 'The laws about the Sabbath teach us to honor God and to rest from our labors.'

**132** 'The laws about sacrifice teach us gratitude and devotion to God.'

**133** 'All the laws, taken together, teach us to live in a way that honors God and benefits our neighbors.'

**134** He spoke of justice: 'God requires us to deal justly with all people, without partiality.'

**135** 'We must not take advantage of the poor or the weak, but must defend their rights.'

**136** 'We must be honest in all our dealings and not deceive our neighbors in any way.'

**137** He spoke of the nature of true wisdom: 'Wisdom begins with the fear of God.'

**138** 'The wise man is not the one who has read many books, but the one who has learned to obey God.'

**139** 'True wisdom is shown in action, not in words.'

**140** He spoke of prayer: 'Prayer is not a matter of many words, but of a sincere heart.'

**141** 'God does not need our prayers, but we need to pray, for it disciplines our souls.'

**142** He spoke of the community: 'We are bound to one another as members of one body.'

**143** 'What harms one of us harms all of us, and what benefits one benefits all.'

**144** He spoke of hope: 'Those who suffer for God's sake will be rewarded.'

**145** 'The righteous may suffer in this life, but God will vindicate them in the end.'

**146** He spoke of death: 'Death is not the end, for the soul lives on after the body dies.'

**147** 'Those who have lived righteously will rest in peace, and those who have done evil will face judgment.'

**148** He spoke of the translation: 'It is a great thing that the king wishes to translate our law.'

**149** 'For the law of God is not only for the Jews, but for all people who seek wisdom.'

**150** 'All who read it and follow it will find the path to a good life.'

**151** He blessed the translators and prayed that God would guide their work.

**152** He said: 'May God open your minds to understand the depths of his law.'

**153** 'And may he guide your tongues to express his truth faithfully in another language.'

**154** He gave each of the seventy-two translators his personal blessing and a gift.

**155** The gifts were scrolls of the law, written by the finest scribes in Jerusalem.

**156** They were written on the finest parchment and in the most beautiful script.

**157** Eleazar also sent a letter with the translators to Ptolemy.

**158** The letter praised the king's wisdom and piety in undertaking the translation.

**159** It requested that when the translation was complete, the king treat it with the highest honor.

**160** It also requested that a copy be sent back to Jerusalem for the temple library.

**161** Eleazar said: 'May the God of Israel bless you and keep you, King Ptolemy.'

**162** 'May he prosper your kingdom and protect it from all enemies.'

**163** 'And may the translation of his law bring wisdom and blessing to all who read it.'

**164** We departed from Jerusalem with great joy and with a deep sense of the importance of our mission.

**165** The road back to Alexandria was long, but our hearts were light.

**166** We spoke much along the way of what we had seen and heard.

**167** We were all moved by the holiness and wisdom of Eleazar and the beauty of the temple.

**168** We were also moved by the devotion of the priests and the people to their law.

**169** I reflected much on what I had seen, and I was filled with a new respect for the Jewish people.

**170** Their devotion to their God and their law is something that puts many other peoples to shame.

**171** We arrived back in Alexandria filled with enthusiasm for the task ahead.

**172** The vestments of the High Priest are of extraordinary beauty and symbolic meaning.

**173** The breastplate contains twelve precious stones, one for each tribe of Israel.

**174** On the stones are engraved the names of the twelve patriarchs.

**175** The golden bells on the hem of the garment ring as the High Priest moves.

**176** The robe is of blue and purple and scarlet and fine twisted linen.

**177** On the hem are pomegranates of blue and purple and scarlet and fine linen.

**178** The ephod is of gold and blue and purple and scarlet and fine twisted linen.

**179** On the shoulder pieces are two stones of onyx, with the names of the twelve tribes engraved on them.

**180** The golden diadem on the High Priest's head bears the sacred Name.

**181** When the High Priest is dressed in his full vestments, he appears more than human.

**182** The splendor of his appearance inspires reverence in all who behold him.

**183** The garments are not merely beautiful — they are full of symbolic meaning.

**184** Each element of the vestments represents an aspect of the priestly calling.

**185** The High Priest wears these garments when he enters the sanctuary to make atonement.

**186** He represents before God all the people of Israel when he stands in the holy place.

**187** The king asked: 'How can a king be most powerful?' The scholar replied: 'By ruling himself first, and by doing justice to all. For the ruler who controls himself and deals justly will be honored by all his subjects.' The king was greatly pleased by this answer.

**188** The king asked: 'What is the finest thing a king can do?' The scholar replied: 'To honor God and to do justice to all men, for these two things bring the greatest glory.' The king was greatly pleased by this answer.

**189** The king asked: 'What is wisdom?' The scholar replied: 'Wisdom is knowing the things of God and of men, and applying that knowledge to the benefit of all.' The king was greatly pleased by this answer.

**190** The king asked: 'What is strength?' The scholar replied: 'True strength is the mastery of oneself, for one who cannot govern himself cannot govern others.' The king was greatly pleased by this answer.

**191** The king asked: 'What is the greatest honor a man can receive?' The scholar replied: 'The love of those over whom he rules, for this is a gift that cannot be bought.' The king was greatly pleased by this answer.

**192** The king asked: 'How should a king treat his friends?' The scholar replied: 'As he would wish to be treated by them — with loyalty, honesty, and generosity.' The king was greatly pleased by this answer.

**193** The king asked: 'What is the most important thing in life?' The scholar replied: 'To know God, for all other good things flow from that knowledge.' The king was greatly pleased by this answer.

**194** The king asked: 'How should a king deal with enemies?' The scholar replied: 'With justice, not with cruelty. The wise king seeks to make friends of his enemies where possible.' The king was greatly pleased by this answer.

**195** The king asked: 'What brings the most grief to a man?' The scholar replied: 'A guilty conscience, for it gives no rest by night or by day.' The king was greatly pleased by this answer.

**196** The king asked: 'What brings the greatest happiness?' The scholar replied: 'Virtue, for it brings contentment that neither wealth nor power can give.' The king was greatly pleased by this answer.

**197** The king asked: 'How should a king treat the poor?' The scholar replied: 'With the same justice as the rich, for God has made all men equal in soul.' The king was greatly pleased by this answer.

**198** The king asked: 'What is the best preparation for a king before making a great decision?' The scholar replied: 'Prayer and reflection, for God gives wisdom to those who seek it with humility.' The king was greatly pleased by this answer.

**199** The king asked: 'How should a man bear misfortune?' The scholar replied: 'With patience and trust in God, for all things are in his hands.' The king was greatly pleased by this answer.

**200** The king asked: 'What is the nature of friendship?' The scholar replied: 'True friendship is built on virtue, and will endure all things.' The king was greatly pleased by this answer.

**201** The king asked: 'How should a king conduct himself in public?' The scholar replied: 'With dignity and consistency, for his people look to him as a model.' The king was greatly pleased by this answer.

**202** The king asked: 'What should a king do to maintain peace?' The scholar replied: 'Practice justice and show mercy, for these are the foundations of peace.' The king was greatly pleased by this answer.

**295** When the translators arrived in Alexandria, the king received them with great honor and prepared a place for them to work on the island of Pharos.

**296** The island was provided with everything necessary, and the translators worked in complete comfort and peace.

**297** They worked in groups and compared their translations, so that the final result represented perfect agreement among all seventy-two.

**298** The translation was completed in exactly seventy-two days, which was understood as a sign of divine providence.

**299** When the king heard that the work was done, he was overjoyed and praised the translators greatly.

**300** He read aloud from the completed translation, and all who heard it were astonished at its beauty and accuracy.

**301** The completed translation was brought before the assembled Jewish community in Alexandria.

**302** The priests, elders, and people listened as the translation was read to them.

**303** When they had heard it, they expressed great admiration and declared it to be an accurate and beautiful rendering of the Hebrew scriptures.

**304** They pronounced a curse on anyone who should alter the translation in any way.

**305** They said: 'This translation was made under divine guidance, and to change it would be to tamper with the word of God.'

**306** The king rejoiced greatly and ordered the translation to be placed in the royal library with the highest honor.

**307** He gave the translators magnificent gifts and allowed them to return to Jerusalem.

**308** Each of the seventy-two received three sets of fine garments, two talents of gold, a golden cup, and a bed.

**309** They also received letters of commendation to the High Priest Eleazar, praising their work.

**310** The king wrote to Eleazar: 'The work of your scholars has been a great benefit to this kingdom and to all the world.'

**311** 'We have placed the translation in our royal library as the most honored of all our books.'

**312** 'We ask that you pray for us and for our kingdom.'

**313** Eleazar, receiving the letter, was greatly pleased and gave thanks to God for inspiring the king.

**314** He replied: 'May the God of Israel bless and keep you, and may your kingdom prosper in peace.'

**315** And so the account of the translation of the law of Moses into Greek comes to its end.

**316** This is what I myself witnessed, Philocrates, and I have set it down faithfully for you.

**317** I have neither exaggerated nor omitted anything of importance, but have told it as it happened.

**318** If you wish to learn more about the nature of the Jewish law, you should read it for yourself.

**319** For in that law is contained all the wisdom that any person could need for a good and righteous life.

**320** The God who gave the law is the God of all people, even though not all people have yet come to know him.

**321** My prayer is that more and more people will come to know him, and that his law will be honored by all nations.

**322** May God bless all who seek him in truth. This is the end of the letter of Aristeas to Philocrates.
